q-94766.name: Question 1
q-94766.problem:
Given that $A$ is a $5\times 5$ real symmetric matrix, which of the following statements are true?

I. $A$ must have $5$ distinct eigenvalues

II. $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable

III. If $u$ and $v$ are two eigenvectors that correspond to the same eigenvalue, then $u⊥v$
q-94766.worked_solution:
Given that $A$ is an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix over $R$, the spectral theorem states the following:

- The eigenvalues of $A$ are all real.

- Eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

- The dimension of the eigenspace for each eigenvalue equals the multiplicity of that eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial.

- $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. According to the spectral theorem, the eigenvalues are real but not necessarily distinct. This occurs when the characteristic polynomial has roots whose (algebraic) multiplicity is greater than $1.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, any symmetric matrix with real entries is orthogonally diagonalizable.

- Statement III is false. According to the theorem, eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues must be orthogonal, but two eigenvectors that correspond to the same eigenvalue may not be orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

q-95702.name: Question 4
q-95702.problem:
Given that $A$ is a $7\times 7$ real symmetric matrix whose roots of the characteristic polynomial have multiplicity equal to $1,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. If $u$ and $v$ are two eigenvectors that correspond to the same eigenvalue, then $u$ is parallel to $v$

II. $A$ must have $7$ real and distinct eigenvalues

III. $A$ is orthogonal
q-95702.worked_solution:
Given that $A$ is an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix over $R$, the spectral theorem states the following:

- The eigenvalues of $A$ are all real.

- Eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

- The dimension of the eigenspace for each eigenvalue equals the multiplicity of that eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial.

- $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. According to the theorem, eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues must be orthogonal. But two eigenvectors that correspond to the same eigenvalue will always be parallel if the geometric multiplicity of the eigenvalue is $1.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix are real. Also, since the roots of the characteristic polynomial have (algebraic) multiplicity all equal to $1,$ the eigenvalues are all distinct.

- Statement III is false. According to the theorem, any symmetric matrix with real entries is orthogonally diagonalizable, but not necessarily orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

q-140847.name: Question 6
q-140847.problem:
Suppose that

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$

are eigenvectors of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=8,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$
q-140847.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}]+8\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}]+8\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}]+8\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]+8\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-140846.name: Question 7
q-140846.problem:
Suppose that

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$

are eigenvectors of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$
q-140846.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}]+1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}]+1\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}]+1\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]+1\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-95730.problem:
Suppose that

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$

are eigenvectors of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$
q-95730.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$

q-95729.problem:
Suppose that

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]$

are eigenvectors of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-24,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$
q-95729.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}5 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-24)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-24)\cdot \frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{26}(2\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-24)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -5\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{26}(2\cdot [\begin{aligned}25 & 5 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]+(-24)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 25\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}26 & 130 \\ 130 & -598\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 5 & -23\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-95718.name: Question 10
q-95718.problem:
Suppose that

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$

are eigenvectors of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=13$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-12,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$
q-95718.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =13\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4\end{aligned}]+(-12)\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =13\cdot \frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 4\end{aligned}]+(-12)\cdot \frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}(13\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 4\end{aligned}]+(-12)\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 3\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{25}(13\cdot [\begin{aligned}9 & -12 \\ -12 & 16\end{aligned}]+(-12)\cdot [\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-75 & -300 \\ -300 & 100\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -12 \\ -12 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

v1=[−34] and v2=[43]

are eigenvectors of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A that correspond to the eigenvalues λ1=13 and λ2=−12, respectively. Find the matrix A.

The spectral decomposition of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A is given by

A=λ1u1⋅u1T+λ2u2⋅u2T, where u1 and u2 are orthonormal eigenvectors of A corresponding to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2, respectively.

u1=v1‖v1‖=15[−34]u2=v2‖v2‖=15[43]

q-140848.name: Question 11
q-140848.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}].$
q-140848.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-95712.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -4 & 18\end{aligned}].$
q-95712.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -4 & 18\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ -4 & 16 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=4{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{17}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{17}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{17}[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-95705.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 6 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}].$
q-95705.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 6 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{13}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-95704.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =5.$ Computing $A-5I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{5}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-95707.name: Question 15
q-95707.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =8$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}].$
q-95707.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =8.$ Computing $A-8I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-8I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 \\ -5 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 & 0 \\ -5 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The spectral decomposition of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A is given by

A=λ1u1⋅u1T+λ2u2⋅u2T, where u1 and u2 are orthonormal eigenvectors of A corresponding to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2, respectively.

Moreover, ui⋅uiT is the projection matrix corresponding to ui.

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ=8. Computing A−8I, we get

A−8I=[3−5−53]−8[1001]=[−5−5−5−5].

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−x2. Hence, the general solution is
